chunks.section: GistRank : Gist-Compressed Listwise Ranking with Large Language Models
chunks.text: Guo Chen Affiliation: Southwest University Affiliation: Yuanbao Team, Tencent Wenhan Liu Affiliation: Renmin University of China Reed Li Affiliation: Yuanbao Team, Tencent Qianwen Ma Affiliation: Yuanbao Team, Tencent Yu Lu Affiliation: Yuanbao Team, Tencent Haibo Shi Affiliation: Yuanbao Team, Tencent Bingbing Xu Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Junjie Huang Affiliation: Southwest University

Large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful tool for listwise relevance ranking, which can improve web search by comparing retrieved passages jointly. However, processing every candidate verbatim and generating a permutation autoregressively can make inference costly, every candidate must be serialized verbatim into the prompt and the input therefore grows linearly with both the number and the length of the passages. While sliding-window ranking handles context limits through repeated re-encoding of overlapping blocks, hard compression techniques sacrifice the fine-grained details required for accurate discriminative judgment. To better understand and mitigate this trade-off, we conduct a comprehensive study of soft compression for LLM-based listwise ranking. Our findings reveal that a vanilla gist representation is ill-suited to ranking for two reasons: strictly causal encoding weakens how thoroughly each gist token absorbs its passage, and the representation is never trained to expose the relative-preference structure that separates closely competing candidates. To this end, we propose GistRank , a three-stage training framework that equips a large language model with gist-compressed passage representations by learning faithful gist tokens under a semi-bidirectional attention scheme, instilling discriminative comparison through pairwise training, and adapting the model to the listwise objective. GistRank collapses each passage into only K = 4 K{=}4 gist tokens, this gives 14 × \times speedups over one-shot full-text ranking while reaching 59.17 average nDCG@10 over TREC DL19/20 and five BEIR subsets within 0.89 of the strongest full-context baseline. Overall, GistRank provides an effective means to enhance efficiency for searches in real-world environments.

Large language models have rapidly become a powerful tool for relevance ranking, where a single model is prompted with a query alongside an ordered list of candidate passages and asked to directly emit the permutation that best reflects their relevance ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; liu2026training ) . This listwise formulation lets the model reason jointly over all candidates and exploit cross-passage comparisons that pointwise and pairwise scorers cannot capture, and it has proven so effective that the capability of proprietary models has been distilled into compact open-source rankers that now serve as strong and reproducible baselines ( Pradeep et al., 2023a ; Pradeep et al., 2023b ) . Driven by these successes, listwise ranking with large language models has quickly become a central paradigm in modern retrieval pipelines. However, in web search and retrieval-augmented applications, the response must also be produced within an inference budget. A conventional listwise reranker serializes the candidate passages into the ranking prompt. Its input grows with both the number and length of passages, even when the entire list fits inside the model’s context window ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . A long candidate list, or passages that are individually long, quickly inflates inference latency, degrading both ranking quality and responsiveness. As shown in Figure 1 , the prevailing remedy is to process the list through a sliding window that reranks overlapping blocks and propagates the ordering across passes ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025d ) , but this comes at the cost of repeatedly re-encoding overlapping content. These costs motivate reducing the information consumed by the ranking stage, while explicitly accounting for any work needed to prepare that information.

Figure 1: Comparison of existing listwise ranking strategies: Sliding Window, Full Ranking and GistRank , corresponding to panels (a), (b), and (c), respectively. A promising solution is to compress each passage before ranking, for example, extracting a summary or embedding the passage ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Besides, a family of soft-compression methods encodes long inputs into a handful of trainable gist tokens that retain the conditioning effect of the original text while drastically shortening the sequence ( Mu et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2023 ) . We argue that such compression is a natural fit for improving inference efficiency in ranking tasks, as it could replace each verbatim passage with a compact set of gist tokens. Prior work has in fact measured gist and KV-level compression on reranking and reported a large gap to full attention ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , but has treated that gap as an intrinsic cost of compression. We argue it is instead a feature of the compression objective: relevance judgment hinges on fine-grained, query-conditioned distinctions among closely competing candidates, whereas objectives optimised for reconstruction or generative conditioning are never asked to preserve those distinctions. In ranking, the compressed states must expose relative preference across candidates, not merely preserve a useful account of each passage. Bridging this gap therefore requires adapting the gist representation so that it preserves the discriminative signals on which ranking depends.

We propose GistRank , which equips a large language model with compressed gist tokes passage representations for efficiency listwise ranking through a three-stage training procedure. In the first stage, we learn faithful gist representations: fixed-length documents are followed by a set of gist tokens that are in turn concatenated with the query, with the query trailing the gist tokens. The model is trained to predict the subsequent tokens conditioned solely on the gist, while granting the gist tokens richer bidirectional access to their source context. In the second stage, with the gist tokens visible, but the original documents hidden, we train these representations on real-world search engine interaction data with pairwise objectives, instilling the discriminative capability required to distinguish competing candidates for the purpose of ranking. In the third stage, we continue training the model directly on labeled ranking data, so that it learns to leverage the gist tokens to produce the listwise permutation both efficiently and accurately.

We evaluate both relevance and inference cost rather than treating a shorter prompt as proof of a faster complete pipeline. Over TREC DL19/20 and five BEIR subsets, GistRank obtains 59.17 mean nDCG@10. GistRank has total end-to-end P50 latencies of 1,625 ms on DL19 and 1,634 ms on DL20. Relative to the one-shot full-text baseline these correspond to 14.05 × \times and 13.93 × \times speedups. The measurement includes compression, KV assembly, and ranking. Direct stage measurements show that the compact rank forward accounts for only about 7% of the model time: most work remains in candidate compression. This confirms that compressed segments can significantly reduce overhead during the inference phase. These results highlight the potential of gist-compressed ranking for scalable search applications. Our main contributions are threefold: • We articulate the mismatch between gist objectives for compact conditioning and the relative-preference information required for listwise relevance ranking, and use it to motivate ranking-aware training. • We propose GistRank , a three-stage training method that first learns compressed gist representations, then continues training on real-world search engine data to enhance discriminative ability, and finally adapts gist tokens to efficient listwise ranking. • We evaluate both ranking effectiveness and end-to-end latency on TREC DL19/20 and five BEIR subsets, demonstrating substantially lower latency than the controlled full-text baselines while maintaining competitive average nDCG@10.

In this section, we position GistRank at the intersection of listwise ranking and soft context compression, focusing on how discriminatively trained gist tokens can improve ranking efficiency while preserving effectiveness.

Ranking a candidate set as a whole rather than scoring documents in isolation has long been recognized as a principled formulation, and the earliest learning-to-rank approaches directly optimized list-level objectives that account for the relative ordering among all candidates ( Cao et al., 2007 ; Xia et al., 2008 ; Burges, 2010 ) . With the advent of pretrained language models, this paradigm was reframed as estimating relevance from deep contextualized interactions between a query and each document, first through cross-encoders that score pairs pointwise and then through sequence-to-sequence formulations ( Nogueira and Cho, 2019 ; Nogueira et al., 2020 ; Zhuang et al., 2024 ) . The emergence of large language models pushed this further by feeding an entire ordered list of passages into a single prompt and instructing the model to emit a permutation, which proved remarkably effective even in zero-shot settings and was subsequently distilled into smaller open models for practical deployment ( Reddy et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent methods have taken both accuracy and efficiency into account—for instance, sliding-window-based approaches ( Sun et al., 2023 ) , as well as those utilizing reinforcement learning or collaborative ranking ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025c ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . In real-world retrieval, deploying listwise rankers requires both strong ranking performance and manageable inference costs. Yet existing token-level listwise methods have largely overlooked gist tokens trained with a discriminative ranking objective as a way to compress passage representations while retaining ranking-critical information.

Using soft context compression for model inputs has become an effective way to reduce the computational overhead of model inference. A line of work has sought to shorten the context consumed by a language model by encoding long inputs into a handful of trainable soft tokens, where the seminal approach learns dedicated gist tokens that compress an entire instruction into a compact prefix while preserving its conditioning effect on subsequent generation ( Mu et al., 2023 ) . Building on this idea, later efforts scaled the compression to arbitrary contexts by training autoencoding objectives that reconstruct the original text from a few memory slots, or by recursively summarizing long documents into accumulated soft prompts that extend the effective context length ( Chevalier et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2023 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) . More recent studies have pushed the compression ratio to extreme regimes ( Petrov et al., 2025 ; Tarasov et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2026 ) , and integrated such condensed representations into retrieval-augmented pipelines to reduce the cost of conditioning on retrieved evidence ( Li et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) . Furthermore, research has already extended pre-sorting compression to the token level in an effort to improve efficiency ( Zhi et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . However, these works are primarily optimized for tasks such as representation compression or generative guidance, while capabilities regarding discriminative comparison tasks have been overlooked. There has no research repurposed gist-style soft tokens as compact passage representations for ranking.

A gist trained only to predict text is encouraged to retain information sufficient for that prediction. Relevance ranking asks a different question: which of several candidate passages better satisfies this query? Passages may both contain terms that make the query predictable while differing in the specific evidence needed to order them. For example, a query about the cause of a condition may be predictable from passages that mention the condition, even if only one passage supplies the requested causal evidence. The representation must expose the distinction that affects their relative order, not just the shared topic.

As shown in Figure 2 , GistRank trains the same backbone in three stages: (i) query-predictive gist learning, (ii) pairwise preference training on search interactions, and (iii) listwise ranking adaptation. The gist token learned in earlier stages is reused throughout. Figure 2: Overview of the training workflow. Stage 1 trains the ability to compress gist tokens. Stage 2 involves continued training to enhance discriminative capabilities using search data. Finally, Stage 3 aligns the model with listwise ranking objectives.

We utilized the TREC DL 2019 ( Craswell et al., 2020 ) and TREC DL 2020 ( Craswell et al., 2021 ) datasets for our evaluation experiments, and also employed various datasets from the BEIR benchmark ( Thakur et al., 2021 ) for performance comparisons. Specifically, we selected five publicly available subsets from the BEIR collection (including Covid, DBPedia, SciFact, NFCorpus and Touche) to conduct evaluations.

For the primary efficiency experiments, we used Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as the base model and performed Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on the same training set using two approaches: full-context ranking and ranking based on a summary extracted via BM25 for each passage. Each SFT model was implemented in both full-context and sliding-window variants, serving as direct benchmarks for efficiency. Regarding performance experiments, in addition to the basic BM25 Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) baseline, we included the following models for comparison spanning pointwise, sliding-window, full-context, and embedding-based approaches: monoBERT (340M) ( Nogueira and Cho, 2019 ) , monoT5 (220M) ( Nogueira et al., 2020 ) , RankT5 (3B) ( Zhuang et al., 2024 ) , RankVicuna (7B) ( Pradeep et al., 2023a ) , RankZephyr (7B) ( Pradeep et al., 2023b ) , FullRank 100 (7B) ( Liu et al., 2025d ) , and PE-Rank BM25 (7B) ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . MonoBERT, monoT5, RankT5, PE-Rank and FullRank were trained on annotated query-passage pairs from the MS MARCO training set, whereas RankVicuna and RankZephyr were derived from ranking lists generated by GPT-4.

We evaluate our method from two perspectives: efficiency and retrieval quality. For efficiency, we report three metrics: • P50 latency (ms/query) is the median end-to-end wall-clock time per query, reflecting the responsiveness perceived by users in online serving. • TFLOPs/query is the number of floating-point operations per query, expressed in trillions, indicating how effectively a method utilizes the available compute. • Relative latency is the ratio of a baseline’s P50 latency to that of GistRank under the same evaluation environment. For effectiveness, we adopt nDCG@10 , which jointly assesses the relevance and the ranking order of the top-10 retrieved results, rewarding methods that place highly relevant documents near the top of the list.

We adopt Qwen3-4B-Base as the backbone to study efficient listwise reranking with a compact open-source language model. The backbone provides a 32k context window. For Stage 3, we reuse the MS MARCO-based candidate lists and GPT-4o-annotated teacher permutations provided by Liu et al. (2025d) , using a single training epoch by default. The controlled full-text, summary, and gist variants use the same Stage 3 training examples and teacher permutations. We compress each passage into 4 gist tokens, and adopt a listwise ranking window of size 100 100 . The model is optimized with a micro batch size of 1 1 and a global batch size of 8 8 , using a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} . Training is conducted on a single node with 8 × \times H20 GPUs using the DeepSpeed framework ( Rasley et al., 2020 ) and bfloat16 mixed precision. In this section, we conduct efficiency experiments on DL19 and DL20 to verify that GistRank substantially accelerates listwise ranking, which is the central motivation of this work. Specifically, we rerank the top-100 passages retrieved by BM25 and compare three ranking regimes: the conventional sliding window (with a window size of 20 and a step size of 10), full ranking that consumes the entire list in a single pass, and our gist-token ranking. As controlled full-context baselines, we build two SFT variants on the same Qwen3-4B backbone as GistRank : one that serializes every passage verbatim, and one that first condenses each passage into a BM25-extracted summary. We report end-to-end P50 latency, TFLOPs per query, and relative latency with respect to GistRank . When calculating the TFLOPs for GistRank , we report both the computational cost associated with the padding process and the computational cost attributed to the actual padded tokens.

Table 1 reports the corrected SFT efficiency measurements on DL19 and DL20. One-shot full-list ranking consistently achieves lower latency than sliding-window ranking. On DL19, processing the full list reduces P50 latency from 43,304 ms to 22,827 ms, and using BM25 passage summaries further lowers it to 18,312 ms. The corresponding DL20 latencies are 32,093 ms, 22,760 ms, and 18,305 ms. These results suggest that repeated processing of overlapping passages and input length both contribute to ranking latency. GistRank compresses the candidates into gist states and performs joint ranking in one non-autoregressive forward pass, with total P50 latencies of 1,625 ms on DL19 and 1,634 ms on DL20, including candidate compression and KV assembly. Relative to one-shot full-text ranking, these latencies give 14.05 × \times /13.93 × \times speedups; relative to full-text sliding-window ranking, the factors are 26.65 × \times /19.64 × \times . The corresponding factors for summary-based one-shot and sliding-window ranking are 11.27 × \times /11.20 × \times and 25.95 × \times /18.72 × \times , respectively. The gains reflect the complete inference procedure, including batched candidate compression and non-autoregressive ranking, rather than the isolated effect of shortening the rank prompt. Therefore, GistRank demonstrates a significant efficiency advantage throughout the entire inference process.

In this section, we evaluate the ranking effectiveness of GistRank . We rerank the top-100 passages retrieved by BM25 and report nDCG@10 on seven datasets, including the two TREC deep-learning sets DL19 and DL20 as well as five BEIR subsets covering diverse domains, namely TREC-COVID, DBPedia, SciFact, NFCorpus, and Touché. We compare against a broad set of baselines that spans pointwise, sliding-window, full-context, and embedding-based models, and further include two Qwen3-4B variants trained under full-context and summary-based settings. Finally, we report the nDCG@10 results for each subset, as well as the average performance across the seven datasets.

The results are presented in Table 2 . Despite compressing each passage into only a few gist tokens, GistRank achieves an average nDCG@10 of 59.17, ranking second among all evaluated methods and trailing the strongest baseline, FullRank 100 , by 0.89 points. On the in-domain TREC datasets, GistRank achieves the highest score on DL19 at 73.88 and the second-highest score on DL20 at 70.82. These results suggest that compact gist representations retain relevance information needed for effective ranking. Compared with the Qwen3-SFT-Full baselines built on the same backbone, GistRank improves average nDCG@10 by 1.37 points over sliding-window ranking and 2.00 points over full-list ranking, demonstrating that its compact representations support competitive effectiveness even when compared with methods that retain the original passage text. In Section 5.4 , we establish a more direct performance reference by employing a full-text rank slot variant based on the uncompressed outputs from Stage 2. The comparison with Qwen3-SFT-Summary further highlights the effectiveness of learned soft compression: GistRank exceeds the summary-based baselines by 6.83–7.65 points on average. This gap suggests that learned gist representations preserve ranking-relevant information more effectively than BM25-extracted summaries. On the out-of-domain five BEIR datasets, performance varies across domains, but GistRank remains competitive on Covid and DBPedia, achieving scores of 82.42 and 43.20, respectively. Its overall average also exceeds those of the evaluated baselines, although individual methods retain advantages on particular datasets. These results indicate that GistRank can significantly reduce ranking latency while still maintaining robust overall ranking performance.

Table 3 examines the contribution of Stage 2 and the effectiveness retained by gist compression. Since Stage 3 provides the listwise training required by the final ranking task, we retain it in both gist variants and ablate only Stage 2. Removing Stage 2 reduces average nDCG@10 from 59.17 to 56.68, a decrease of 2.49 points, with degradation across all seven datasets. The largest drop occurs on DL20, from 70.82 to 66.55, followed by SciFact, from 75.46 to 72.74. These consistent improvements suggest that learning to compress passages in Stage 1 does not fully capture the discriminative information needed for ranking, and that the citation-derived preference supervision in Stage 2 provides a useful initialization for subsequent listwise training. At the same time, the variant without Stage 2 remains competitive after Stage 3, indicating that Stage 2 strengthens ranking effectiveness rather than being a prerequisite for learning the ranking task.

This demonstrates that our method is robust to the ordering of input positions.

We analyze the inference cost of GistRank by separating candidate compression, KV assembly, and joint ranking. Latency measurements cover the complete reranking pipeline, from processing the query and candidate passages to producing the final ranked candidate list. Table 4 shows that candidate compression dominates inference latency, accounting for approximately 92.9% of total time on both datasets. Its mean latency is 1,450.23 ms on DL19 and 1,463.74 ms on DL20, whereas joint ranking requires only 110.39 ms and 110.69 ms, respectively. KV assembly contributes less than 0.1% of total time. Including all three stages, total P50 latency is 1,624.66 ms on DL19 and 1,634.37 ms on DL20. These results show that gist representations make listwise ranking inexpensive, with query-conditioned candidate encoding accounting for most of the remaining overhead. The computation breakdown follows the same pattern. Candidate compression requires 149.09 and 150.59 TFLOPs/q on DL19 and DL20, accounting for approximately 94% of total estimated operations. Joint ranking requires only 9.56 and 9.57 TFLOPs/q, bringing the totals to 158.66 and 160.16 TFLOPs/q. Although these totals exceed those of the one-shot baselines, GistRank achieves lower latency through batched candidate compression and joint ranking over compact gist states. The stage-wise results identify candidate compression as the main target for further latency improvements.

To isolate the general representational capacity of gist tokens, we remove the explicit query q q from the Stage 3 ranking format and retrain the model while keeping all other settings fixed. This diagnostic evaluates whether the compressed passage states themselves remain useful for ranking. In this section, we quantify the rank-stage token cost to explain, at the token level, why GistRank is both faster and more predictable than the baselines. As shown in Table 6 , we measure the rank-stage prompt length on DL19 and DL20 for N = 100 N{=}100 passages. At the per-passage level, serializing a passage verbatim consumes about 79 tokens and a BM25 summary about 26, whereas GistRank represents each passage with only 4 gist tokens in the rank phase. This propagates to the full listwise rank input: over the N = 100 N{=}100 candidates, the median full-text prompt spans more than 8,000 tokens on both DL19 and DL20 and the summary prompt around 3,000, while GistRank needs only about 1,250. This result shows that GistRank drastically reduces the context length of the listwise rank phase. A more distinctive property of GistRank is that every candidate contributes exactly K K gist slots regardless of its raw length. This near-constant rank-phase length makes the downstream latency, the KV-cache footprint, and the batching throughput more predictable.

Figure 4 makes this compression concrete by rendering one candidate passage under the three protocols. The full text keeps all 115 tokens, the summary retains only the single sentence that directly answers the query, and GistRank collapses the whole passage into 4 gist tokens. Although the summary happens to preserve the answering sentence, it discards the passage’s discussion of alternative causes that a ranker may need to distinguish this candidate from its competitors; GistRank keeps the discriminative signal that Stage 2 is trained to preserve by a fixed number of gist tokens. By combining a fixed-size ranking representation with competitive ranking performance and low inference latency, GistRank offers predictable rank-stage costs and practical potential for deployment in search systems.

In this paper, we introduce GistRank , a three-stage training framework for gist-compressed listwise ranking. The framework combines query-predictive gist learning, citation-derived pairwise supervision, and listwise adaptation to optimize compact passage representations for relevance ranking. Experiments on TREC DL19/20 and five BEIR subsets show that GistRank achieves competitive average nDCG@10. GistRank reduces reranking latency relative to autoregressive SFT baselines, while approaching the effectiveness of a full-text reference with the same rank-slot scoring procedure. These results highlight the potential of GistRank for efficient deployment in practical search systems. The inference-cost breakdown shows that candidate compression accounts for most of the remaining latency, motivating further optimization of this stage. Future work will investigate query-independent passage compression that allows gist states to be precomputed and reused across queries.
